newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: New housing curbs to hit Singapore property market.
newsitem.headline: New housing curbs to hit Singapore property market.

text.p: Singapore's new curbs on public housing purchases will likely dampen sentiment towards the residential property market, already dented by growing oversupply, property analysts said on Monday.
Over the weekend, the Singapore government announced changes to the mortage financing policy for purchases of public-housing flats from the Housing Development Board (HDB).

Among the changes are new credit assessment criteria for HDB buyers to make sure they buy within their means, and a requirement that families with monthly incomes of more than Singapore $8,000 (US$5,555) pay market interest rates.
Under the government's current housing subsidy, HDB buyers pay just 3.58 percent for a mortgage loan from the HDB against the 6.75 to seven percent from commercial banks.
Property analysts said the measures were less severe than expected but would still hurt sentiment toward the private residential market, already suffering from sluggish sales.

"The measures by themselves are only mildly negative. But put in the context of an oversupply situation building up in the private market, prices will be further under pressure," said Lim Chung Chun, investment analyst with ING Baring Securities.
Leong Chi Meng, investment analyst with Vickers Ballas, said the direct impact of the moves would be to bring the selling of public housing units more in line with market practice.
"It will also prevent abuse of the subsidised housing loans offered by the HDB," he said.
Singapore has a highly successful public housing scheme that houses about 86 percent of the population, and about 90 percent of these flats are owned by those who live in them.
With growing affluence, many HDB owners have been selling public housing flats to upgrade to private homes. This upgrading also has the effect of supporting prices in the private market.

Lim said private developers have so far resisted cutting prices in the residential market even as the stockpile of unsold units built up. He said developers launched 5,000 new units in the last half of 1996 but sold just over 3,000 new units.
Lim said he expected the trend to continue this year where about 12,000 new private homes are expected to be launched.
"Sentiment will definitely become more cautious," said Lim.
Vickers' Leong said sentiment for property stocks will continue to be "jittery" judging by the strong sell-down in property stocks on Friday ahead of the new HDB curbs.
"The residential market is still quite uncertain. Our house call is to avoid stocks with heavy residential exposure," he said.
